chunk_findings.detail: `close()` only sets `self.closed = True`; it leaves `self.connected` true. `_guarded()` gates calls on `connected`, not `closed`, so a closed client still answers. With `c = FakeMcpClient(); c.connect(1); c.close(); c.list_tools(1)`, the last call returns an OK outcome (tools/list) instead of `UNAVAILABLE`, so any test of post-close behavior or of the closed flag is wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpClient.close

chunk_findings.detail: `connect()` sets `self.connected = True` before checking `reply.status`. If the initialize reply is an error, the method returns a failed `Handshake` but leaves the client marked connected. For a stub server whose `handle` returns `W.err(msg["id"], W.INTERNAL_ERROR, "bad")` for `initialize` and a normal reply for `tools/list`, `c.connect(1)` returns status `ERROR`, yet `c.list_tools(1)` does not return `UNAVAILABLE` and proceeds to call the server. A failed handshake should leave the client disconnected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpClient.connect

chunk_findings.detail: The constructor/docstring says `results` may map a tool name to “an Exception to raise”, but `handle()` only special-cases `W.ToolError`. Given `FakeMcpServer(tools=[{"name": "x"}], results={"x": RuntimeError("boom")})`, a `tools/call` for `x` returns `W.ok(mid, RuntimeError("boom"))` (a successful JSON-RPC result containing an exception object) instead of raising or returning an error. Thus scripted exception results do not exercise the error/`serve` exception path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: When `intercept(msg, self.notify)` returns `True`, `serve` executes `continue` before the `after()` block, so the documented contract that `after()` “runs once per message, answered or not” is violated. For example, `StdioServer(...).serve([{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "ping"}], intercept=lambda msg, notify: True, after=counter)` leaves the counter at `0` even though one message was processed by the interceptor; any caller using `after` for per-message bookkeeping or ratchets will undercount offloaded calls.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.serve

chunk_findings.detail: In the `OSError` branch, `connect` returns `Handshake(UNAVAILABLE, detail=...)` without passing the caller’s requested `version` into `protocol`. Thus `StdioClient(starter=raise OSError, argv=["x"]).connect(1.0, version="2024-11-05")` reports `handshake.protocol.offered == "2025-03-26"` (the default `OFFER_VERSION`) instead of `"2024-11-05"`, corrupting the protocol-version fact for an unavailable server.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioClient.connect

chunk_findings.detail: `receive` appends each read chunk and immediately trims the accumulated buffer with `_keep` before checking for a newline. If the buffer is at or near `_MAX_BUF`, that trim can discard the newline that terminated a complete JSON-RPC line. For example, after `_MAX_BUF` bytes of an initialize response have been read without a newline, a subsequent `os.read` can return `\n` followed by another 64 KiB of data; `_keep` drops the first 64 KiB of the combined buffer, including that newline, so the reader never sees the line terminator and times out even though the server answered. The buffer should be split into lines first and only the remaining partial line trimmed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:_ProcessChannel.receive

chunk_findings.detail: The AST guard intended to forbid the default adapter from importing another ddflow layer misses relative imports. `ast.ImportFrom` stores the dotted path without leading dots and records relative depth in `level`; for example, `from ..services import probe` yields `module='services'` and `level=2`, and `from . import probe` yields `module=''`/`None`. The comprehension at line 194 produces `'services'` or `''`, which does not start with `ddflow` or `.` and is not `subprocess`, so the assertion passes. Thus adding a relative ddflow import such as `from ..services import probe` to `ddflow/adapters/mcp.py` would not be caught by this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapters_mcp.py:199

chunk_findings.detail: `after()` is documented as running “once per message, answered or not,” but when `intercept(msg, self.notify)` returns True the loop `continue`s before the `after` call. A normal `tools/call` message that `intercept` takes over will therefore never run `after`. If the caller uses `after` to mark an offloaded call complete (which is the apparent purpose given `surfaces/mcp/_serve.py` was modified to add `intercept` and `after`), this leaves the call/state outstanding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.serve

chunk_findings.detail: After a successful JSON-RPC `initialize` response, `connect` sends `notifications/initialized` unconditionally. Given a server result of `{"protocolVersion": "2030-01-01"}` (outside `SERVED_VERSIONS`), `negotiate` correctly returns `supported=False`, but the client still sends `initialized` and reports `status == OK`. The adapter thereby continues the MCP initialization flow for a protocol revision it declares unsupported, letting a caller later use `list_tools`/`call` on a connection that failed version negotiation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioClient.connect

chunk_findings.detail: The server does not enforce JSON-RPC request validity. A top-level JSON value that is not an object, e.g. the line `"not-a-frame"`, receives `-32602 INVALID_PARAMS`; JSON-RPC 2.0 specifies `-32600 Invalid Request`. Likewise `handle` accepts and executes requests missing `"jsonrpc": "2.0"`. This makes the wire adapter reject/accept invalid peers with the wrong wire-level semantics.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.serve, StdioServer.handle

chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:verify_one

chunk_findings.detail: The AST scan fails to detect relative imports because `ast.ImportFrom` stores the leading dots in the `level` field, not in `module`. For example, `from . import registry` yields `module=None`, so the expression `(n.module or "")` becomes `""`; the assertion’s `m.startswith(".")` check is never triggered. As a result, a prohibited relative import inside `ddflow/adapters/mcp.py` would be silently accepted, defeating the test’s stated guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapters_mcp.py:test_the_default_adapter_imports_no_other_ddflow_layer_and_no_subprocess

chunk_findings.detail: `after` is not run when `intercept` returns `True`: the loop executes `continue` before the `after()` block. The port’s serve contract (as documented for the default adapter and mirrored by this fake) is that `after` runs once per message, answered or not. Given `srv = FakeMcpServer(); calls = 0; srv.serve(['{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"ping"}'], intercept=lambda msg, notify: True, after=lambda: increment(calls))`, `calls` remains `0` even though one message was handled by the interceptor. If `after` is used to mark an offloaded/intercepted call complete, this fake leaves that bookkeeping state outstanding and diverges from the real adapter.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.serve

chunk_findings.detail: `params = msg.get("params") or {}` assumes `params` is a mapping. Given `FakeMcpServer().handle({"id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": [1]})`, the method raises `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` instead of returning `W.err(1, W.INVALID_PARAMS, ...)`. When the same frame is processed through `serve`, the exception is caught and reported as `-32603 internal error`, so malformed JSON-RPC params are misclassified as an internal/transport failure rather than invalid params.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `encode()` uses `json.dumps(frame)` with Python’s default `allow_nan=True`, so it can emit `NaN`, `Infinity`, or `-Infinity`, which are not valid JSON and therefore not valid JSON-RPC/MCP wire frames. For example, `encode(ok(1, {"x": float("nan")}))` returns a string containing `NaN`; a strict JSON parser on the peer will reject the line, corrupting the stream. This can be reached from normal tool use: a tool result or a client `call(..., {"x": float("nan")})` passes through `encode` and produces an invalid frame instead of failing closed or serializing to a JSON-valid value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:encode

chunk_findings.detail: `handle()` still accepts and executes requests that are not valid JSON-RPC 2.0 requests because it does not require `msg["jsonrpc"] == "2.0"` or a present `method` field. For example, a line containing `{"id": 1, "method": "ping"}` is answered as a successful `ping`, and `{"jsonrpc": "1.0", "id": 1, "method": "ping"}` is also answered successfully; JSON-RPC 2.0 requires `-32600 Invalid Request` for such requests. This remains true in the current code and gives the wrong wire-level error semantics for invalid peers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: When `intercept(msg, self.notify)` returns True, the loop `continue`s before the `after()` call, so intercepted messages never trigger `after`. Example: `calls=[]; FakeMcpServer().serve(['{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"ping"}'], intercept=lambda msg, notify: True, after=lambda: calls.append(1))` leaves `calls == []`. Since this fake is the in-memory stand-in for the same conformance cases as the default adapter and `after` is documented there as running once per message answered or not, this is the same contract violation as the previously reported `StdioServer.serve` bug, now at this new server.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.serve

chunk_findings.detail: `_ask` calls `self.server.handle` directly and never catches an exception. `FakeMcpServer.handle` now deliberately raises non-`W.ToolError` exceptions so that `serve` can map them to a `-32603` error, but the fake client bypasses `serve`; therefore a scripted server error escapes as a raw Python exception from public `call`. Example: `server=FakeMcpServer(tools=[{"name":"x"}], results={"x": RuntimeError("boom")}); c=FakeMcpClient(server); c.connect(1); c.call("x", {})` raises `RuntimeError` instead of returning an `Outcome` with `status=W.ERROR`/an internal-error result, so the fake pair does not emulate the wire adapter’s error outcome.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpClient._ask

chunk_findings.detail: The new params normalization silently treats any non-dict `params` as an empty params object: `params = msg.get("params") if isinstance(msg.get("params"), dict) else {}`. This avoids the earlier `AttributeError`, but it no longer models invalid-params wire behavior. For example, `FakeMcpServer().handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": [1]})` returns a successful `initialize` result with a negotiated protocol version instead of `W.err(1, W.INVALID_PARAMS, ...)`. The same happens for `tools/list` with array params: the fake returns the declared tool table as if the request were well-formed. A conformance or regression test that feeds a malformed JSON-RPC params value through the fake will therefore see a successful response and can hide a real bug in the adapter or caller.

Given `encode(ok(1, {"x": float("nan")}))`, the returned line contains `NaN` (and similarly `Infinity` / `-Infinity`), which is not valid JSON and therefore not a valid JSON-RPC/MCP frame. This can be reached from normal tool use, e.g. a tool result or a client `call(..., {"x": float("nan")})`; a strict JSON parser on the peer rejects the line and the stream desynchronizes. chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #4 still holds: `handle` does not enforce the JSON-RPC 2.0 request shape. It accepts a frame with no `jsonrpc` field, or with `jsonrpc != "2.0"`, as long as `id` and `method` match. For example, `StdioServer().handle({"id": 1, "method": "ping"})` returns a successful `ping`, and `{"jsonrpc": "1.0", "id": 1, "method": "ping"}` also returns success; JSON-RPC 2.0 requires `-32600 Invalid Request`. It also silently replaces non-object `params` with `{}`, so `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": [1]}` returns a successful initialize instead of an invalid-params error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `serve` maps any exception from `handler` to a JSON-RPC error without checking whether the message was a notification. Given `StdioServer().serve(['{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"ping"}'], handle=lambda msg: (_ for _ in ()).throw(RuntimeError("boom")))`, the adapter writes an error frame with `id: null`. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires that servers not reply to notifications, even unrecognized or failing ones; this injects an unexpected response into the stream.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff removes `import json`, `_ECHO_MARK`, `_reply_to`, and `_describe_answer`, but the only new code shown in this file is `_ProcessChannel` and `_ProcessStarter`; it does not rewrite the body of `verify_one` to stop using the deleted helpers. Because the body of `verify_one` is unchanged in the diff, it still references those names when building/parsing the JSON-RPC `initialize` exchange. A normal call such as `verify_one(companion)` therefore raises `NameError` (e.g. `name 'json' is not defined` or `name '_reply_to' is not defined`) instead of returning a `Verification`. This is previous finding #7 still holding: the added process channel/starter classes do not replace the deleted request/response helpers in `verify_one`.

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #8 still holds at this new call site. `intercept` returns `True` for every message selected by `offload and _offloaded(msg)` (lines 61–73), and the only reexec check is inside `after` (lines 75–77). chunk_findings.detail: This new conformance case does not actually enforce “unavailable is never passed” for `call`. Since the same file elsewhere treats `.status` as the authoritative outcome (e.g. `got.status == W.OK`, `unknown.status == W.ERROR`), this test should assert `client.call(...).status == W.UNAVAILABLE`.

This is reachable from a tool result or from `McpClient.call(..., {"x": float("nan")})`.

chunk_findings.detail: `serve` records an error response for malformed frames but then `continue`s before the `after` callback, while every valid JSON-object frame calls `after`. Given `server = FakeMcpServer()`, `after` is never called for `server.serve(["not-json\n", "42\n"], after=after)`, even though `server.sent` gets two error responses. If a test uses `after` to bound an infinite/long line iterator or to assert that each processed frame was handled, malformed input can hang or skip assertions.

chunk_findings.detail: The fake client does not map escaped exceptions the same way `FakeMcpServer.serve` does. Given `FakeMcpServer(tools=[{"name": "t"}], results={"t": ValueError("boom")})` and `FakeMcpClient(server)`, `client.call("t", {}, 1)` returns an outcome whose error message is `"boom"`, but the same exception through `FakeMcpServer.serve` is sent as `"internal error: boom"`. Since the fake client is meant to stand in for the wire path and the comment says it is what `serve` makes of an escaped exception, tests comparing fake client and fake server error messages will fail.

chunk_findings.detail: `describe_answer` copies the whole `serverInfo` object into the returned server facts, and `StdioClient.connect` then negotiates from `server.get("protocolVersion")`. If the initialize result has no top-level `protocolVersion` (or has an empty/falsy one) but its `serverInfo` happens to contain a `protocolVersion` key, the client treats that as the negotiated protocol version. For example, a server that answers `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"serverInfo":{"name":"x","version":"1","protocolVersion":"2025-03-26"}}}` with no top-level `protocolVersion` will make `hello.server["protocolVersion"]` become `"2025-03-26"`, so `negotiate` reports `supported=True` even though the protocol response did not actually declare a protocol version. The negotiation fact should be taken from `result["protocolVersion"]`, not from arbitrary `serverInfo` contents.

chunk_findings.detail: A handler/tool result that is not JSON-serializable aborts the transport instead of being mapped to a JSON-RPC error. In `serve`, `handler(msg)` is called inside `try`, but `self.notify(reply)` is called outside it. If a `tools/call` handler returns, for example, `{"content": [{"type": "text", "text": {1, 2}}]}` (a Python set), `notify` calls `encode`/`json.dumps`, raises `TypeError`, and the serve loop terminates without sending any reply for the request or processing later frames. The adapter is supposed to own framing and map failures to JSON-RPC errors; a bad tool result should not crash the wire loop.

chunk_findings.detail: The module declares `encode` to be “the only encoder, so framing changes in one place,” but `connect` sends the required `notifications/initialized` frame with a direct `json.dumps(...)` call instead of `encode(...)`. If `encode` is later changed to add newline framing, compact separators, or other wire-format details (the stated purpose of this adapter), this one frame will not follow the change and can corrupt the newline-delimited JSON-RPC stream. Use `encode({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"})` here ([r-reuse-core]).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioClient.connect

chunk_findings.detail: `send` writes the full JSON-RPC line synchronously with `proc.stdin.write` and `flush`, with no deadline or non-blocking handling. The configured `timeout_s` is only used later in `receive`, so if a companion process is alive but not draining stdin (for example, blocked on its own upstream or a lock) and the request exceeds the OS pipe buffer, the write blocks until the server reads. A concrete case is a `tools/call` request whose `arguments` payload is larger than the pipe buffer sent to such a server: the client hangs in `send` indefinitely instead of returning the intended timeout/unavailable result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:_ProcessChannel.send

chunk_findings.detail: While waiting for a newline, `receive` trims an unfinished line to the last `_MAX_BUF` bytes, but when a newline finally arrives it returns the remaining bytes as if they were the complete line. Given a legitimate single-line JSON-RPC response longer than 1 MiB (for example, a `tools/list` response with many tools or a large `tools/call` result), the first bytes are discarded after the buffer reaches `_MAX_BUF`; when the server terminates the line with `\n`, `receive` returns only the trailing ~1 MiB. The client then parses a truncated response (or a wrong object if the tail happens to parse) rather than reporting a line-too-long/unavailable condition.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:_ProcessChannel.receive

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor removes the `threading.Lock` that previously serialized all stdout writes, and the writer callback passed to `StdioServer` (`lambda line: (outp.write(line + "\n"), outp.flush())`) is not itself synchronized. The offload path hands this `send`/`notify` callback to background workers via `_offload`, so worker threads can emit JSON-RPC frames concurrently with the main loop and with each other. For example, if two offloaded `tools/call` requests cause their workers to send progress/result frames at the same time, the two `outp.write` calls can interleave in the OS buffer and produce a malformed stdout line such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"content":[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,...` (or split a frame across lines), which the MCP client will reject as a parse error.

chunk_findings.detail: `handle` identifies notifications solely as frames without `"id"` and never checks that the frame is a JSON-RPC 2.0 envelope (`msg.get("jsonrpc") == "2.0"`). A server line `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{},"error":{"code":-32600,"message":"x"}}` is accepted, and `_exchange` then returns status `OK` because of the `"result"` branch. JSON-RPC forbids both members in one response, so this malformed response is misreported as a successful initialize instead of being not-a-response.

chunk_findings.detail: The timeout only bounds `receive`, not `send`. `_exchange` calls `self._send(encode(frame))` before ever checking the deadline. With a `Channel` whose `send` writes synchronously to a pipe and a server that never reads stdin, a large `tools/call` arguments line can fill the pipe and block in `send` past `timeout_s`, causing `call()` or `connect()` to hang indefinitely despite the advertised "bounded in time" semantics.

chunk_findings.detail: `select.select([fd], [], [], left)` uses the POSIX `select()` interface, which raises `ValueError: filedescriptor out of range in select()` when the child’s stdout pipe `fd` is `>= FD_SETSIZE` (for example when the ddflow process already has 1024 or more open file descriptors before spawning the companion). This channel should use `selectors.PollSelector` or `select.poll`, which is not limited to 1024 descriptors.

chunk_findings.detail: In `test_serve_answers_through_the_table_and_runs_the_hooks`, the line assigns `after=lambda: after.append(1)`. chunk_findings.detail: `connect` decides `Negotiation.supported` from `hello.server.get("protocolVersion")`, but `describe_answer` copies the whole `serverInfo` object into `server` and only overrides `protocolVersion` when the top-level `result.protocolVersion` is truthy. The three-valued negotiation is wrong: silence/absence of `result.protocolVersion` should be `None`, not `True` inferred from `serverInfo`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:describe_answer / StdioClient.connect

chunk_findings.detail: If the server echoes our request and then closes, the code reports `EOF`, not `ECHOED`. For example, with a `Channel.receive` that first returns `encode(initialize_request(1))` and then raises `EOFError`, `_exchange` sets `echoed = True` from `_is_echo`, but the `except EOFError` branch unconditionally returns `done(EOF, ...)`. The documented `echoed` status (“our request came straight back (not a server)”) is lost, conflating an echo/cat-style process that closes with a silent server that closed before answering.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioClient._exchange

chunk_findings.detail: `send` performs a blocking write/flush to the child's stdin with no timeout or non-blocking handling. If the MCP client uses this channel for a request whose encoded line is larger than the OS pipe buffer (for example a `tools/call` with large arguments) to a companion process that does not consume stdin (e.g. a `sleep`-like process), `proc.stdin.flush()` blocks indefinitely. The timeout passed to `receive` is never reached, so the client hangs instead of returning the intended timeout/unavailable result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:_ProcessChannel.send

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback path assumes `starter.proc` is always a real process object. If `W.StdioClient` is replaced by the required fake client for tests, or by any `Client` implementation that does not start a real process, a non-answered result that is not explicitly one of `UNAVAILABLE`, `ECHOED`, `TIMEOUT`, or `CLOSED_BEFORE_READ` (for example, a fake `connect` returning a closed-after-read status to simulate a server that exits after receiving the request) reaches `proc = starter.proc`. The probe should handle a missing process handle or obtain exit information through the client port rather than reaching into the concrete starter.

chunk_findings.detail: `handle` never validates the JSON-RPC `id` type. An input frame such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":{},"method":"tools/list"}` reaches `mid = msg["id"]` as `{}` and is answered with `W.ok({}, ...)`. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires `id` to be a String, Number, or Null, and an invalid request with an invalid id must be answered with an error whose `id` is null. The fake therefore returns a bogus success response for an invalid wire frame instead of `Invalid Request`, so the conformance stand-in for the real adapter encodes the wrong protocol behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: `StdioClient.connect` sends `notifications/initialized` whenever `first.status == OK`, without checking `hello.protocol.supported`. The probe should handle a missing process handle or obtain exit information through the client port rather than reaching into the concrete starter.

chunk_findings.detail: `handle` never validates the JSON-RPC `id` type. An input frame such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":{},"method":"tools/list"}` reaches `mid = msg["id"]` as `{}` and is answered with `W.ok({}, ...)`. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires `id` to be a String, Number, or Null, and an invalid request with an invalid id must be answered with an error whose `id` is null. The fake therefore returns a bogus success response for an invalid wire frame instead of `Invalid Request`, so the conformance stand-in for the real adapter encodes the wrong protocol behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:48 FakeMcpServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `StdioClient.connect` sends `notifications/initialized` whenever `first.status == OK`, without checking `hello.protocol.supported`. A server that answers `initialize` with `protocolVersion: "2099-01-01"` (a version not in `SERVED_VERSIONS`) sets `hello.protocol.supported` to `False`, but the client still sends the initialized notification. That tells an incompatible server to begin operating under a revision this wire does not serve; version negotiation should stop before initialized is sent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:401

chunk_findings.detail: `self._send(...)` is called for the `notifications/initialized` notification and its return value is ignored. If the server closes the stream immediately after sending its `initialize` response, this write raises `OSError`, `_send` returns `False`, but `connect` still returns the `Handshake` created from `first` with `status == OK`. The caller is told initialization succeeded even though the required notification was never written, and the next call will hit the broken channel.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:401

chunk_findings.detail: The diff deletes `_reply_to`, `_describe_answer`, `_ECHO_MARK`, and the `json` import, while the hunk stops at the `def verify_one(...)` line without changing the function body. That body is the prior implementation and still calls the removed `_reply_to`/`_describe_answer` helpers, so any companion probe that invokes `verify_one` (e.g. `verify_one(c)` for a configured companion) raises `NameError: name '_reply_to' is not defined` before the server is started.

chunk_findings.detail: The new branch is meant to preserve the old “exited before reading a request” outcome, but it checks `hello.detail` instead of `hello.status`. The other adapter conditions in this function all check `hello.status == W.*` (`UNAVAILABLE`, `ECHOED`, `TIMEOUT`), while `hello.detail` is used as a human-readable detail string in the `UNAVAILABLE` branch. Given a companion that exits immediately without reading the initialize request (e.g. `/bin/false`), `StdioClient.connect` will report `hello.status == W.CLOSED_BEFORE_READ`, but the string in `hello.detail` will not equal that status constant, so this branch is skipped and the function falls through to the generic “exited 0 without answering `initialize`” message. This regresses the distinct behavior for an immediate-exit command.

chunk_findings.detail: The new JSON-RPC `id` guard accepts booleans because `bool` is a subclass of `int`. Given a parsed frame such as `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": true, "method": 123}`, the check `mid is not None and not isinstance(mid, str | int | float)` is false, so the request is not rejected as an invalid-id request. It falls through to the method check and is answered with `id: true` (for example `{"id": true, "error": ...}`), whereas JSON-RPC 2.0 requires an invalid request with a non-String/Number/Null id to be answered with `id: null`. The same guard in `ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:46` has the same behavior, so the fake used as the conformance stand-in also misanswers.

chunk_findings.detail: The new id-type check uses `isinstance(mid, str | int | float)`, but in Python `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so a JSON-RPC 2.0 frame such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":true,"method":"ping"}` is accepted as valid. JSON-RPC 2.0 permits `id` only as a String, Number, or Null; a boolean `true`/`false` is not a Number and is an invalid request. The added test covers `id: {}` but not `id: true`, so both the real adapter and the conformance fake still return a response with the invalid boolean id instead of an `Invalid Request` error with `id: null`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new params normalization silently treats any non-dict `params` as an empty params object: `params = msg.get("params") if isinstance(msg.get("params"), dict) else {}`. This avoids the earlier `AttributeError`, but it no longer models invalid-params wire behavior. For example, `FakeMcpServer().handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": [1]})` returns a successful `initialize` result with a negotiated protocol version instead of `W.err(1, W.INVALID_PARAMS, ...)`. The same happens for `tools/list` with array params: the fake returns the declared tool table as if the request were well-formed. A conformance or regression test that feeds a malformed JSON-RPC params value through the fake will therefore see a successful response and can hide a real bug in the adapter or caller.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `encode` is the single wire encoder used by both the server and client, but it calls `json.dumps(frame)` with Python’s default `allow_nan=True`. Given `encode(ok(1, {"x": float("nan")}))`, the returned line contains `NaN` (and similarly `Infinity` / `-Infinity`), which is not valid JSON and therefore not a valid JSON-RPC/MCP frame. This can be reached from normal tool use, e.g. a tool result or a client `call(..., {"x": float("nan")})`; a strict JSON parser on the peer rejects the line and the stream desynchronizes. Previous finding #3 still holds.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:encode

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #4 still holds: `handle` does not enforce the JSON-RPC 2.0 request shape. It accepts a frame with no `jsonrpc` field, or with `jsonrpc != "2.0"`, as long as `id` and `method` match. For example, `StdioServer().handle({"id": 1, "method": "ping"})` returns a successful `ping`, and `{"jsonrpc": "1.0", "id": 1, "method": "ping"}` also returns success; JSON-RPC 2.0 requires `-32600 Invalid Request`. It also silently replaces non-object `params` with `{}`, so `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": [1]}` returns a successful initialize instead of an invalid-params error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `serve` maps any exception from `handler` to a JSON-RPC error without checking whether the message was a notification. Given `StdioServer().serve(['{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"ping"}'], handle=lambda msg: (_ for _ in ()).throw(RuntimeError("boom")))`, the adapter writes an error frame with `id: null`. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires that servers not reply to notifications, even unrecognized or failing ones; this injects an unexpected response into the stream.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.serve

chunk_findings.detail: The diff removes `import json`, `_ECHO_MARK`, `_reply_to`, and `_describe_answer`, but the only new code shown in this file is `_ProcessChannel` and `_ProcessStarter`; it does not rewrite the body of `verify_one` to stop using the deleted helpers. Because the body of `verify_one` is unchanged in the diff, it still references those names when building/parsing the JSON-RPC `initialize` exchange. A normal call such as `verify_one(companion)` therefore raises `NameError` (e.g. `name 'json' is not defined` or `name '_reply_to' is not defined`) instead of returning a `Verification`. This is previous finding #7 still holding: the added process channel/starter classes do not replace the deleted request/response helpers in `verify_one`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:verify_one

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #8 still holds at this new call site. `intercept` returns `True` for every message selected by `offload and _offloaded(msg)` (lines 61–73), and the only reexec check is inside `after` (lines 75–77). Given an offloaded `tools/call` that causes `srv.reexec_pending` to become true and `_reexec_ready(inp, relays)` to become true, the upgrade path is bypassed if `StdioServer.serve` skips `after()` when `intercept` returns `True`, as reported in the prior round. The diff moves the check into `after` but does not make it run for intercepted/offloaded messages, so `_upgrade.execute(srv, PROC.replace_process)` can still be missed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp/_serve.py:79

chunk_findings.detail: This new conformance case does not actually enforce “unavailable is never passed” for `call`. It asserts only `client.call("echo", {}, 1).answered is False`; a client implementation that returns `W.OK` with `answered=False` before `connect()` would pass this test even though the call is being reported as passed rather than unavailable. Since the same file elsewhere treats `.status` as the authoritative outcome (e.g. `got.status == W.OK`, `unknown.status == W.ERROR`), this test should assert `client.call(...).status == W.UNAVAILABLE`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapters_mcp.py:test_calls_before_connect_are_unavailable_not_passed

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #2 is only partially answered: the `AttributeError` is gone, but a malformed `params` value is still not rejected. `params = msg.get("params") if isinstance(msg.get("params"), dict) else {}` silently coerces any non-object `params` into `{}`. For example, `FakeMcpServer().handle({"id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": [1]})` now returns `W.ok(1, {...})` and announces a successful initialization, instead of returning `W.err(1, W.INVALID_PARAMS, ...)`. A client sending invalid structured params during `initialize` is therefore treated as a valid handshake, not a protocol error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:45 FakeMcpServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `encode()` calls `json.dumps(frame)` with Python’s default `allow_nan=True`, so it can emit `NaN`, `Infinity`, or `-Infinity`, which are not valid JSON and therefore not valid JSON-RPC wire frames. For example, `encode(ok(1, {"x": float("nan")}))` produces a line containing `NaN`; a conforming peer will reject that line, corrupting the stream. This is reachable from a tool result or from `McpClient.call(..., {"x": float("nan")})`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:encode

chunk_findings.detail: `StdioServer.handle` still dispatches messages without requiring `msg["jsonrpc"] == "2.0"` or a present, string `method` field. A line such as `{"id": 1, "method": "ping"}` is answered as a successful `ping`, and `{"jsonrpc": "1.0", "id": 1, "method": "ping"}` is also answered successfully; `{"id": 1}` reaches `METHOD_NOT_FOUND` rather than `-32600 Invalid Request`. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires `-32600` for these malformed requests.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: The diff removes `import json`, `_ECHO_MARK`, `_reply_to`, and `_describe_answer`, but adds only `_ProcessChannel` and `_ProcessStarter`; it does not rewrite `verify_one`. That function’s unchanged body still depends on the deleted helpers to build and parse the `initialize` request, so a normal call such as `verify_one(companion)` raises `NameError` (for `_reply_to`/`_describe_answer`/`json`) instead of returning a `Verification`. This is previous finding #7 still holding: the new helper classes do not replace the removed parse/describe logic.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/probe.py:verify_one

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #8 still holds at this new call site. The `intercept` callback returns `True` for every message selected by `offload and _offloaded(msg)`, and `after()` is the only place where `srv.reexec_pending` / `_reexec_ready` is checked. `StdioServer.serve` skips `after()` when `intercept` returns `True`, so an offloaded `tools/call` that makes a pending reexec ready never triggers `_upgrade.execute`. Example: with `offload=True`, `srv.reexec_pending=True`, and an offloaded `tools/call` whose relay finishes such that `_reexec_ready(inp, relays)` becomes true, `intercept` returns `True`; no later unoffloaded message is required for the protocol state to be ready, but `after` is not run for this frame and the upgrade is never executed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp/_serve.py:transport.serve(inp, srv.handle, intercept=intercept, after=after)

chunk_findings.detail: The new request-shape validation still does not reject a missing `method` field. Because both handlers bind `method = msg.get("method", "")`, a frame such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1}` passes the `not isinstance(method, str)` check as the empty string and then falls through to `METHOD_NOT_FOUND` (`method not found: `) instead of the JSON-RPC 2.0 `-32600 Invalid Request` required for a request object missing its required `method` member. The same logic is duplicated in `FakeMcpServer`, so the fake mirrors the malformed-request behavior rather than enforcing the port’s conformance rule.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle (and ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.handle)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `id` validation accepts JSON booleans as valid JSON-RPC request ids because `bool` is a subclass of `int`: `isinstance(True, str | int | float)` is true. Given a frame parsed from `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": true, "method": "ping"}` (or the equivalent fake-server call), `handle` passes the id check and dispatches the method instead of returning `-32600 Invalid Request`; if the method is invalid, it can also emit a response whose `id` is `true`, which is not a valid JSON-RPC 2.0 id. The added test covers `{}` but not `true`/`false`, so this malformed-request case still passes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle (and ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.handle)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `id` validation `isinstance(mid, str | int | float)` treats `bool` as a valid JSON-RPC id, because Python `bool` is a subclass of `int`. JSON-RPC 2.0 only permits String, Number, or Null for `id`; `true`/`false` are not Numbers. A wire request such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":true,"method":"ping"}` therefore passes validation and is answered successfully with the boolean id echoed back, producing an invalid JSON-RPC response frame (`"id": true`). It should instead be rejected as `INVALID_REQUEST` with `id: null`. The same defect exists in both the real adapter and the fake.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:StdioServer.handle and ddflow/adapters/fakes/mcp.py:FakeMcpServer.handle

chunk_findings.detail: `valid_id` accepts non-finite floats as valid JSON-RPC ids: `valid_id(float("nan"))` and `valid_id(float("inf"))` return `True` because `isinstance(..., float)` is true. Given a parsed request such as `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": float("nan"), "method": "ping"}` (Python’s default `json.loads` accepts `NaN`), `StdioServer.handle` does not reject it as `INVALID_REQUEST`; it returns a response frame whose `id` is `NaN`. The shared `encode` then emits `"id": NaN` (or `Infinity`), which is not valid JSON and therefore not a valid JSON-RPC/MCP wire frame, corrupting the stream for strict peers and breaking response matching for Python clients because `NaN != NaN`. The fake server inherits the same behavior via `W.valid_id`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:valid_id

chunk_findings.detail: `valid_id` still accepts `float("nan")`, `float("inf")`, and `float("-inf")` as valid JSON-RPC ids because they satisfy `isinstance(mid, float)`. Those Python values are not JSON numbers, so a request id of `NaN`/`Infinity` is not a valid JSON-RPC 2.0 id. Python's default `json.loads` parses the non-standard tokens `NaN` and `Infinity`, so a frame such as `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": NaN, "method": "ping"}` reaches `handle`, passes `valid_id`, and is dispatched; the response then echoes the NaN id and `encode` (which keeps `json.dumps` defaults) emits a line containing `NaN`, which is invalid JSON. It should be rejected with `INVALID_REQUEST` and `id: null`. The new bool check fixed only `True`/`False`, not non-JSON float values.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/mcp.py:valid_id
